Grade 3 · Unit 3.2

Weather, Climate, and Hazards

What weather can we expect in different places and seasons, and how can we reduce harm from weather hazards?

Concept 1

Weather is short-term; climate is long-term

Weather is what happens today; climate is the pattern over many years.

Analogy

Mood vs personality

two faces: “today” and “usually.”

“Weather is your mood today. Climate is what people expect most of the time.”

Data

Daily vs monthly

one day temperature card vs many-year average.

“One day can be weird. Many years show climate.”

Concept 2

We measure weather

Scientists measure temperature, precipitation, wind, and clouds.

Try it

Rain gauge

cup with ruler.

“After rain, measure how deep the water is.”

You did this before / what is new: You noticed weather in K-B; now you measure it and record data.

Try it

Wind vane

paper arrow on pencil.

“A wind vane points into the wind. The wind comes FROM that way. Put the tail on the other end.”

Real world

Weather report

weather map icons.

“Symbols show rain, snow, sun, and wind.”

Concept 3

Graphs show seasonal weather patterns

Tables and graphs show typical weather by month or season.

Diagram

Monthly bar graph

bars for monthly high temperatures.

“July bars are tall. January bars are short.”

Try it

Graph your class data

student-entered temperatures or precipitation.

“Make a bar for each month.”

Data

Provided Michigan weather dataset

a table of typical monthly temperature and precipitation for a Michigan city.

“Use the numbers. Make bars. Find the warm months and cold months.”

Concept 4

Different regions have different climates

Climate depends on location, including nearness to large lakes or oceans.

Diagram

Climate map

simple map with cold, temperate, and hot regions.

“Near the equator is warmer. Near the poles is colder.”

Data

Region cards

cards for a tropical place, a polar place, and a Michigan place.

“Combine the clues. What is usually true there?”

Real world

Michigan and the Great Lakes

Michigan surrounded by lakes.

“The Great Lakes make Michigan weather milder near shore and snowier in some places.”

Concept 5

Designs can reduce weather-hazard harm

Solutions such as barriers, drains, and rules can reduce damage, but they cannot remove all risk.

Analogy

Helmet

bicycle helmet.

“A helmet does not stop falls. It reduces harm.”

Try it

Barrier test

soil slope, water, cardboard/foil barriers.

“Test barriers. Which one keeps soil in place?”

You did this before / what is new: You used fair tests in Unit 0; now you test a flood-barrier solution.

Data

Before/after erosion

measured sediment with and without barrier.

“Less sediment means the barrier helped.”

Try it

Claim frame

sentence frame on paper.

“I claim ___ reduces harm from ___ because our data show ___.”

Hands-on · Design or investigate

Try it at home or in class

Test a flood-barrier design. Use the same amount of water each time. Compare how much soil moves. Then write: “I claim ___ reduces harm from flooding because our data show ___.”

Try it

What you need

paper cup, ruler, straw, paper, tape, pencil, thermometer if possible, shallow tray, soil or sand, small cardboard or foil barriers, craft sticks, spoon.

Safety: wash hands after soil or sand trays.

Try it

What you do

make a rain gauge and wind vane; record daily weather; graph class data or provided data; compare climate cards; test a flood barrier with the same amount of water each time.

No time or no good weather? Use this data

This data is a backup. It lets you practice reading evidence, but the standard expects you to collect your own when you can.

daily or weekly weather calendar.

typical average daily HIGH temperature by month for Detroit, Michigan, rounded to the nearest degree (a given year can differ by several degrees): Jan 32°F, Feb 35°F, Mar 45°F, Apr 58°F, May 69°F, Jun 79°F, Jul 83°F, Aug 81°F, Sep 74°F, Oct 62°F, Nov 50°F, Dec 38°F; precipitation about 2.0, 1.9, 2.4, 3.0, 3.0, 3.2, 3.1, 3.2, 3.0, 2.6, 2.7, 2.2 inches. Backup barrier dataset: no barrier moves 8 spoonfuls of sediment; grass model moves 2; cardboard fence moves 5. GUESS for exact numbers, STRONG for the seasonal pattern.

Near you: Lake-effect snow: cold air moves over warmer Great Lakes water, picks up moisture, and drops heavy snow on nearby land.

Words to know

weather
short-term condition of the air.
climate
typical weather over a long time.
temperature
how hot or cold something is.
precipitation
rain, snow, sleet, or hail.
wind
moving air.
season
part of the year with typical weather patterns.
pattern
something that repeats.
data
information collected.
hazard
something that can cause harm.
flood barrier
a design that slows or blocks flood water.
Tutor notes: misconceptions, standards, pacing

Pacing: five 30-minute sessions.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • “Weather and climate are the same.” Correct: weather is short-term; climate is long-term.
  • “One cold day means climate changed.” Correct: climate needs long-term patterns.
  • “Seasons happen because Earth is closer to the Sun in summer.” Correct: tilt causes seasons; detailed cause comes later.
  • “Clouds make cold.” Correct: clouds can block sunlight or trap heat.
  • “Hazards cannot be reduced.” Correct: designs can reduce harm, but they cannot eliminate all risk.

Limits and cautions:

  • This unit does not fully teach the water cycle; Unit 4 does that.
  • It does not teach climate change; later units handle human impact.
  • Cause of seasons is simplified here and handled more fully later.
  • Barrier tests are models; real flood control involves engineering, land use, and public policy.

Michigan Science Standards this unit earns:

  • 3-ESS2-1: Represent data to describe typical weather expected by month or season.
  • 3-ESS2-2: Obtain and combine information to describe climates in different regions.
  • 3-ESS3-1: Make a claim about the merit of a design solution that reduces the impacts of a weather-related hazard.
  • 3-5-ETS1-1: Define a design problem with criteria and constraints.
  • 3-5-ETS1-2: Generate and compare solutions.
  • 3-5-ETS1-3: Plan and carry out fair tests.

Connections: Builds on: K-B Sunlight, Weather, and Staying Safe; Unit 0: How Science Works. Builds toward: 5.4 Earth’s Spheres, Water, and Communities; Unit 4 Weather & the Water Cycle; Unit 6 Natural Hazards.
